title: Tighten a rough draft
prompt:
Act as a careful editor. Rewrite the text below so it is clear and about [target length] words, for [audience]. Keep my meaning and my voice. Do not add facts. After the rewrite, list the three biggest changes you made.

Text:
[paste draft]
check: Compare against the original: did any fact, number or promise change?
tip: Paste only text you are allowed to share.

title: Write a polite but firm email
prompt: Draft an email to [recipient and relationship] about [situation]. Goal: [what I want them to do] by [date]. Tone: polite and firm, no blame. Under [120] words. Give me two versions: shorter and warmer.
check: Check names, dates and any commitment before sending.

title: Turn notes into meeting minutes
prompt:
Turn these raw notes into meeting minutes with: decisions, action items (owner and due date), and open questions. If an owner or date is missing, write “unassigned” instead of guessing.

Notes:
[paste notes]
check: Confirm every owner and date against what was actually said.

title: Explain it simply
prompt: Explain [topic] to someone with no background, in plain English, in under [200] words. Use one everyday analogy, then one sentence saying where the analogy breaks down.
check: Verify the key claim in a textbook or trusted source.

title: Make a draft sound more human
prompt:
Rewrite the text below so it sounds like a person speaking: shorter sentences, concrete examples, no buzzwords. Keep every fact. Flag any sentence you could not improve without changing meaning.

Text:
[paste]
check: Read it aloud. Remove anything you would not say.

title: Summarise a long document
prompt:
Summarise the document below in: (1) three-sentence overview, (2) five key points, (3) what is still unclear or missing. Quote the exact sentence for each key point so I can check it.

Document:
[paste]
check: Spot-check at least two quotes against the source.
tip: Quotes make errors easy to catch.

title: Compare two options
prompt: Compare [option A] and [option B] for [my situation] across: cost, effort, risk, and reversibility. Use a table. State your assumptions first and list what you would need to know to be sure.
check: Challenge the assumptions. They are often where it goes wrong.

title: Build a reading list
prompt: I want to learn [topic] from scratch in [4 weeks]. Propose a week-by-week plan with what to read or watch, a small exercise each week, and how I will know I understood. Mark anything you are not sure exists.
check: Check that every named book or resource actually exists.

title: Pre-mortem a plan
prompt: Here is my plan: [plan]. Assume it failed in six months. List the seven most likely reasons, ordered by likelihood, and one early warning sign for each.
check: Pick the top two and decide what you will do about them.

title: Extract data from messy text
prompt:
From the text below, extract a table with columns: [column names]. If a value is missing, leave it blank. Do not infer. After the table, list any rows you were unsure about.

Text:
[paste]
check: Compare 5 random rows against the source.

title: Account research brief
prompt:
Using only the public information I paste below about [company], write a one-page brief: what they do, recent signals, likely priorities, and three questions I could ask. Mark any inference as an inference.

Public information:
[paste]
check: Verify each fact and its date before you mention it to the prospect.

title: First-touch message
prompt: Write a 90-word first message to [role] at [company]. Reference this public signal: [signal and source]. Explain the possible link to [what I sell] in one sentence. End with a low-pressure question. No flattery, no jargon.
check: Remove any claim you cannot link to a public source.

title: Follow-up that adds value
prompt:
Write a follow-up to the message below. Add one genuinely useful thing (a short insight, resource or answer to a likely objection). Keep it under 70 words. Do not guilt-trip.

Previous message:
[paste]
check: Would you appreciate receiving this?

title: Handle an objection
prompt: The prospect said: “[objection]”. Give me three honest responses: one that asks a question, one that shares evidence, one that offers a smaller next step. Do not make claims about our product I have not given you.
check: Only use claims you can back up.

title: Call prep sheet
prompt: I have a call with [name, role] about [topic] tomorrow. From this context: [context]. Give me: goal of the call, five questions, likely objections, and the single next step I want to agree.
check: Edit the questions into your own words.

title: Turn a release into a post
prompt:
Turn the release note below into a LinkedIn post for [audience]. Open with the problem it solves, explain it in plain English, and end with one question. 120 to 160 words. Do not exaggerate.

Release note:
[paste]
check: Check every claim against the official source and link it.

title: Headline variations
prompt: Write ten headline options for an article about [topic] for [audience]. Group them by approach: curiosity, benefit, how-to, contrarian. Flag any that might overpromise.
check: Pick two to A/B test. Remove anything misleading.

title: Repurpose one article
prompt:
Turn the article below into: a 5-point email, three social posts, and a short video script (60 seconds). Keep the same facts and tone.

Article:
[paste]
check: Make sure the three versions do not contradict each other.

title: Audience questions list
prompt: List 20 questions a [audience] would type into a search engine about [topic], grouped by stage: just starting, comparing, ready to act. Do not invent statistics.
check: Check which questions you can answer well from real experience.

title: Brand voice check
prompt:
Here is our brand voice: [3 adjectives and one example paragraph]. Review the draft below and flag every sentence that does not fit, with a suggested rewrite.

Draft:
[paste]
check: Accept changes selectively. The voice should still sound like you.

title: Draft a support reply
prompt:
Draft a reply to this customer message. Use only the approved information below. If the answer is not in it, say what we need to find out instead of guessing. Tone: calm and practical.

Customer message:
[paste]

Approved information:
[paste]
check: A person must review before sending. Check policy and tone.

title: Write a clear SOP
prompt:
Turn this description of how we do [task] into a standard operating procedure: purpose, who does what, numbered steps, common mistakes, and a quick checklist. Ask me questions if anything is unclear.

Description:
[paste]
check: Walk through it with someone who does the task.

title: Find the repeated work
prompt: Here is a list of what my team did last week: [paste]. Group the tasks, point out what repeats, and suggest which two are the best candidates to simplify or automate and why. Note the risks.
check: Validate with the people who actually do the work.

title: Summarise a ticket thread
prompt:
Summarise this support thread in five lines: customer problem, what we tried, current status, what the customer is waiting for, and the next step with an owner.

Thread:
[paste]
check: Check for anything sensitive before sharing the summary.

title: Weekly status update
prompt: Write a weekly update from these bullet points for [audience]: [paste]. Structure: progress, risks, decisions needed, next week. Keep it under 150 words. Do not soften real risks.
check: Make sure risks are stated plainly.

title: Practice quiz
prompt: Create a 10-question quiz on [topic] at [level] with an answer key and a one-line explanation for each answer. Do not include trick questions. Tell me which topics are best learned from a textbook rather than from you.
check: Check the answer key against your course notes.

title: Study plan
prompt: I have [number] days before [exam]. Topics: [list]. I can study [hours] per day. Make a day-by-day plan with review sessions and a lighter final day.
check: Adjust it to your real energy and schedule.

title: Teach it back
prompt: I will explain [topic] in my own words. Act as a curious beginner: ask one question at a time, point out where I am vague, and do not correct me until I have finished. Then tell me what I got right and what I missed.
check: Compare their feedback with your notes.

title: Lesson outline
prompt: Create a [45]-minute lesson outline on [topic] for [age/level]. Include a starter, a main activity, a check for understanding and a take-home task. List the learning objective first.
check: Check accuracy and age-appropriateness before use.

title: Career practice
prompt: Act as an interviewer for a [role] position. Ask me one question at a time. After each answer, give two strengths and one improvement. After five questions, summarise my pattern.
check: Treat the feedback as practice, not a prediction.

title: Explain this code
prompt:
Explain what the code below does, step by step, in plain English. Then list any assumptions it makes, inputs that could break it, and anything that looks risky. Do not rewrite it.

Code:
[paste code]
check: Read the code yourself and confirm the explanation matches.
tip: Never paste secrets, keys or proprietary code you are not allowed to share.

title: Write tests for a function
prompt:
Write tests for the function below using [framework]. Cover normal cases, edge cases (empty, null, very large) and one failure case. Explain what each test protects against. Do not change the function.

Function:
[paste]
check: Run the tests. A test that passes proves nothing until you have seen it fail.

title: Review a change for risk
prompt:
Review the diff below as a careful reviewer. List: possible bugs, security concerns, missing tests, and anything unclear. Rank by severity. If you are not sure, say so rather than guessing.

Diff:
[paste]
check: Treat it as a second pair of eyes, not the approver. A person decides.

title: Debug from an error
prompt:
Here is an error and the relevant code. Give me the three most likely causes ranked by probability, and for each the quickest check that would confirm or rule it out. Do not propose a fix until I confirm the cause.

Error:
[paste]

Code:
[paste]
check: Run the checks in order. Do not apply a fix you do not understand.

title: Draft a job description
prompt: Draft a job description for a [job title] at a [company type] in [location]. Include: purpose of the role, 5 key responsibilities, must-have versus nice-to-have skills, and a short, honest note on what makes the role hard. Use inclusive language and avoid unnecessary requirements.
check: Check that every requirement is genuinely needed and that salary and legal wording follow your policy.

title: Structured interview questions
prompt: Create 8 structured interview questions for a [job title], each with: what it assesses, what a strong answer includes, and a red flag. Use the same questions for every candidate. Avoid questions about protected characteristics.
check: Review for fairness and legal compliance with your HR lead before use.

title: Variance commentary
prompt: Write a short commentary explaining this variance for a non-finance reader: [budget vs actual figures and known causes]. Separate what the numbers show from what is assumed. List two questions to ask the budget owner. Do not invent causes.
check: Check every figure and cause against the source before sharing.
tip: Use anonymised or approved figures only.

title: Polite payment reminder
prompt: Draft a payment reminder email for an invoice that is [number] days overdue to [recipient and relationship]. Tone: firm but respectful. Include the invoice details I give you only: [invoice number, amount, due date]. Offer one way to resolve any issue.
check: Confirm the invoice details and your contract terms before sending.

title: Reusable support macro
prompt:
Turn the resolved ticket below into a reusable support reply template with placeholders for customer-specific details. Keep it under 120 words, friendly and clear, and add a one-line internal note on when NOT to use it.

Resolved ticket:
[paste]
check: A person approves macros before they are used with customers.

title: Help-centre article
prompt:
Turn this resolved issue into a help-centre article: a one-sentence summary, symptoms, steps to fix, what to do if it still fails, and who to contact. Write for a non-technical customer.

Issue and fix:
[paste]
check: Test the steps yourself and remove anything you cannot verify.

title: Build an onboarding week plan
prompt: Create a welcoming first-week onboarding plan for [role] at a [company type]. Include a day-by-day schedule, owner, purpose, and links/placeholders for policies. Use only these supplied details: [details]. Flag missing information; do not invent policies.
check: Confirm policy links, owners, accessibility needs, and local requirements before sharing.
tip: Use a fictional role and company details for the first draft.
exampleInput: Role: Customer support associate; start date Monday; hybrid team; buddy: Sam.
demoOutput: Monday: Meet your manager and buddy; set up approved tools; review the team handbook. Tuesday: Learn the product and support workflow; shadow two tickets. Wednesday: Practice with sample tickets and review privacy rules. Thursday: Handle low-risk practice cases with a buddy. Friday: Reflect, ask questions, and agree goals for week two. Owners and policy links: confirm with People Ops before sending.

title: Turn a policy into an employee FAQ
prompt: Using only the policy text below, create a plain-language employee FAQ with concise answers. Cite the relevant section for each answer and mark anything the policy does not answer as “Ask HR.” Policy: [approved policy text].
check: Check each answer against the approved policy and have the policy owner approve it.
tip: Remove employee names and confidential details before using.
exampleInput: Policy: Employees may work remotely up to two days per week with manager approval. Requests go through the HR portal.
demoOutput:
Q: Can I work remotely? A: Up to two days per week, with manager approval. (Remote work section)
Q: How do I request it? A: Submit a request through the HR portal. (Remote work section)
Q: Can I work remotely from another country? A: The policy does not say. Ask HR.

title: Summarise anonymised employee feedback
prompt: Summarise these anonymised survey comments into themes. For each theme, include frequency, a representative paraphrase, evidence, and a follow-up question. Keep minority concerns visible. Do not infer who wrote a comment or recommend individual employment actions. Comments: [anonymised comments].
check: Check theme counts against the source; do not use small groups to identify people.
tip: Use approved survey handling and aggregation thresholds.
exampleInput: Comments: “I do not know who approves my work.” “The new approval steps are unclear.” “My manager explains priorities well.”
demoOutput: Themes: unclear approval ownership (2 comments); positive manager communication (1). Follow-up: Which approvals need a named owner? Evidence: two comments mention unclear approval steps.

title: Create a fair performance review discussion guide
prompt: Create a manager discussion guide from these job expectations and the employee’s self-reported examples. Separate observed evidence from questions and avoid rating, ranking, or inferring traits. Include space for the employee perspective and next-step goals. Expectations: [criteria]. Examples: [anonymised evidence].
check: A manager and HR partner must verify context and fairness; do not let AI decide ratings, promotion, pay, or discipline.
exampleInput: Expectation: respond to customer cases within one business day. Example: handled 18 cases; 15 within target; 3 delayed during a system outage.
demoOutput: Evidence to discuss: 15 of 18 cases met the one-day target; three delays coincided with a system outage. Ask: What contributed to the delays, and what support would help? Goal: agree a response-time plan and review it next month.

title: Write a bug report from reproduction notes
prompt: Turn these reproduction notes into a concise bug report with title, environment, prerequisites, steps, expected result, actual result, impact, and unknowns. Do not invent details. Notes: [sanitised notes].
check: Reproduce the issue and verify versions, impact, and steps before filing.
tip: Remove secrets, customer data, and private URLs.
exampleInput: Notes: On staging, after saving profile with empty display name, page spinner never ends. Chrome current. Expected: save validation message. Actual: spinner.
demoOutput:
Title: Profile save hangs when display name is blank
Environment: Staging, current Chrome
Steps: Open profile → clear display name → save
Expected: validation message
Actual: indefinite spinner
Impact: profile cannot be saved in this state
Unknown: affected browsers and server logs.

title: Draft an API endpoint reference
prompt: Using only this API specification, draft endpoint documentation with method, path, auth, parameters, request and response examples, errors, and unresolved questions. Preserve exact field names and mark missing details. Spec: [API spec].
check: Run examples against the implementation or contract tests; verify auth and error codes.
tip: Use synthetic tokens and sample data only.
exampleInput: Spec: POST /v1/tasks; auth required; body {"title":"string"}; returns 201 {"id":"string","status":"queued"}; 400 invalid title.
demoOutput: POST /v1/tasks — Creates a task. Authentication: required. Body: {"title":"string"}. Success (201): {"id":"string","status":"queued"}. Error (400): invalid title. Open question: rate limits are not specified.

title: Plan a safe refactor
prompt: Propose a small, incremental refactor for this code. State current behavior, risks, smallest change, tests to add, and rollback plan. Do not change behavior or assume dependencies not shown. Code/context: [sanitised code and context].
check: Run the existing suite, inspect the diff, and verify behavior before merging.
tip: Avoid pasting proprietary code into unapproved tools.
exampleInput: Context: formatDate is duplicated in two modules; both accept ISO strings.
demoOutput: Plan: extract a shared formatDate helper; preserve ISO input behavior; add tests for valid dates, invalid strings, and timezone boundaries; update one module at a time; compare outputs before and after; rollback by restoring the original helper if behavior changes.

title: Turn a design brief into user flows
prompt: Translate this product brief into 2–3 user flows. For each, list user goal, entry point, steps, decision points, errors/empty states, and assumptions. Do not invent research evidence. Brief: [brief].
check: Validate flows with product requirements and user research; cover error and accessibility states.
tip: Label assumptions separately from observed user evidence.
exampleInput: Brief: A first-time user needs to create a project and invite a teammate.
demoOutput: Flow: Create project — Goal: start a workspace. Entry: empty dashboard. Steps: choose “New project” → enter name → create. States: required-name validation; network error with retry. Assumption: project creation requires a name. Invite teammate is a separate optional next step.

title: Synthesize usability test notes
prompt: Synthesize these usability notes by task. Separate observed behavior, participant quotes, severity, and interpretation. Group repeated issues, preserve dissenting evidence, and suggest follow-up questions—not solutions presented as fact. Notes: [anonymised notes].
check: Check every theme against source notes and sample size; do not generalise beyond participants.
tip: Remove identifying details and obtain consent for research data use.
exampleInput: Notes: 3 participants tried checkout. 2 missed “Apply code”; 1 found it immediately. One said “I expected this beside the total.”
demoOutput: Observed: 2/3 participants did not find “Apply code” on first attempt; 1/3 found it immediately. Quote: “I expected this beside the total.” Interpretation: placement may not match expectations. Follow-up: test a placement near the order total.

title: Critique a screen for accessibility
prompt: Review this screen description or markup against practical accessibility checks: keyboard order, focus, labels, contrast, text resizing, error communication, and screen-reader semantics. Report issue, evidence, impact, and a suggested check. Screen: [description or code].
check: Verify with automated checks and keyboard/screen-reader testing; this is not a conformance certification.
tip: Use the applicable accessibility standard and product context.
exampleInput: Screen: Modal has “X” icon, email field placeholder “Email”, red error text “Invalid”, blue button.
demoOutput: Potential checks: give the close icon an accessible name; add a persistent label to the email field; associate the error with the field and explain how to fix it; verify focus enters the modal, stays inside, and returns to the opener; test contrast for error text and button.

title: Write interface microcopy variants
prompt: Write 3 concise microcopy options for this UI moment. State the user goal, action, and tone. Include loading, empty, success, and error text where relevant. Avoid blame and unsupported promises. Context: [screen and user goal].
check: Check terminology, character limits, localization, and whether each message matches the actual system behavior.
tip: Test with representative users; prefer clear instructions over clever wording.
exampleInput: Context: user imports a CSV; some rows may fail validation.
demoOutput:
Button: “Review import”
Loading: “Checking your file…”
Success: “Import ready. Review 2 rows before adding them.”
Error: “We couldn’t read this file. Use a CSV with a header row and try again.”

title: Create a usability test script
prompt: Create a 20-minute moderated usability test script for [prototype/task]. Include neutral welcome, consent reminder, 3–5 realistic tasks, non-leading follow-ups, and a debrief. Do not teach the interface during tasks.
check: Pilot the script and ensure tasks test the intended questions without leading participants.
tip: Use consented participants and avoid collecting unnecessary personal information.
exampleInput: Prototype: mobile food ordering checkout. Research question: can users find and change pickup time?
demoOutput: Welcome: We are testing the design, not you. You may stop anytime. Task 1: You are ordering lunch for pickup; show how you would choose a time. Follow-up: What were you expecting to happen? Task 2: Change the pickup time. Follow-up: How confident are you? Debrief: What felt unclear? What would you change?

title: Turn a design brief into a component checklist
prompt: Convert this feature brief into a UI inventory and component checklist. Include states (default, hover, focus, disabled, loading, error, empty), responsive behavior, content needs, and dependencies. Mark open questions. Brief: [brief].
check: Compare checklist with the design system and engineering constraints; confirm responsive breakpoints.
tip: Keep proposed patterns consistent with the existing product design system.
exampleInput: Brief: Search a library of saved reports and pin favorites.
demoOutput: Inventory: Search input; report list item; pin button; empty state; loading skeleton; no-results state. States: focus-visible, disabled while loading, error with retry. Responsive: confirm list layout at mobile widths. Open question: can users pin more than one report?
